entry.title: Mac OS 27 Finder Bar 1.0.0
entry.content:
Mac OS 27 Finder Bar

A Windhawk mod that adds a macOS 27-style menu bar to the top of the screen in Windows 11: the menus of the app in front on the left, and system status, Control Center, notifications and the clock on the right, all in live glass.

Available in English, Português, Español, Français, Deutsch, Italiano and 中文（简体）. The language follows Windows automatically, or can be picked in the settings.

Left side

  • Logo menu: About This PC, System Settings, Microsoft Store (both with pending update counts), Force Quit, Show Desktop, Sleep, Hibernate, Restart, Shut Down, Lock Screen, Sign Out and Menu Bar Settings…
  • Active app name (shown as Finder for the desktop and File Explorer, a name you can change): hide the app, hide others, open file location, close window, quit, force quit
  • Global menu:
    • apps with a classic menu bar (Win32): the app's real menus
    • modern apps: the app's menu bar read through UI Automation when it exists
    • browsers, File Explorer, Office, VS Code and other apps: ready-made menus that send the app's own keyboard shortcuts
    • a Window menu with the app's open windows
  • Help menu with a search across all the app's menus; ← → move between menus (optional Ctrl+F2 opens the bar from the keyboard)

Right side

  • Display: dark mode, night light, projection modes
  • Keyboard layout (when there is more than one), emoji, on-screen keyboard
  • Battery (percentage, charging, time remaining), Wi-Fi (current network, available and known networks), Bluetooth and Sound (scroll on the icon to change the volume, right-click to mute, switch output and input)
  • Now Playing: the song name scrolls across the bar when it doesn't fit; the panel has a large-cover or compact layout and a progress bar drawn as a line, a colored line or a wave
  • Focus (when Do Not Disturb is on), Search (Windows Search or Siri Plus Launchpad), microphone and camera (the icons turn orange and green while an app uses them, as on the Mac; click to see which apps use them and mute the microphone), Weather (Open-Meteo, MET Norway or wttr.in, no account needed) and the Notifications button
  • Clock: the calendar and your agenda from your own .ics files, imported right from the settings window. Date and time formats are configurable
  • An arrow collapses the icons that don't fit; each icon can be turned on or off in the settings

Control Center

Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, media playing, dark mode, Do Not Disturb, brightness, sound and audio output, plus tiles you can add: night light, airplane mode, screenshot, screen recording, power mode, energy saver (one click turns it on and off), magnifier, lock screen, calculator, Task Manager, emoji and show desktop.

  • Edit Controls lets you add, remove, move and resize tiles
  • Clicking power mode opens a box under Edit Controls, as wide as the panel, with the Windows 11 power modes and power plans (repeated plans are hidden)
  • Tile names that don't fit scroll when the mouse is over the tile
  • Tiles can be pills or rounded squares; a tile that is on shows a colored circle or turns into a whole white pill
  • Optional: blur and dim the screen while the Control Center is open; cascade or fade animation when it opens

Notice pills

Small glass pills drop from the bar for headphones, audio output, low battery, charger, Focus, Caps Lock, USB devices and drives, finished downloads, copy and cut, screenshots and screen recordings. Pills you can act on (open and edit a screenshot or recording, open a download, reply to a message) stay 2.5 times longer and are kept in the bell panel; the rest only show in the pill. Volume, brightness and Bluetooth changes can show as floating pills too. The pill's style (glass, liquid glass or dark), size, position, duration and opening and closing animations are all configurable.

Notifications

Turn on Windows notifications in logo → Menu Bar Settings… → Notice pills (off by default) and the bar shows your apps' notifications:

  • in the pill and in the bell panel, grouped by app
  • reply to messages (like WhatsApp) right from the pill, when the app supports replies
  • drag a notification aside in the panel to clear it
  • Only the bar shows notifications: optional; Windows' own banners move off the screen while the bar shows them, and come back when the option or the mod is turned off

Bar and glass

  • Bar background: fully transparent (default), Windows blur glass, or liquid glass (experimental); opaque when the active app is maximized (optional)
  • Live glass: panels blur what's behind them in real time, with an experimental liquid glass with edge refraction (on by default)
  • Menus use their own frosted glass (with a transparency slider) or the same glass as the Control Center
  • Light, dark or automatic theme, nine selection colors for the bar and menus, font, font size, icon size and bar height
  • Hides with full-screen apps, can hide automatically until the mouse touches the top, and shows on every monitor (each optional)

Settings

Logo → Menu Bar Settings… opens a window in the same style as Siri Plus Launchpad: sections on the left with search, every setting applied live without restarting the bar. It's the only place for those settings. Windhawk's settings page has the few the window doesn't: font, glass tints, theme, the name shown for the desktop, ready-made menus, Control Center tile look, opening animation, tray click, the app update count and .ics file paths, plus Reset the bar's settings, which puts the window's options back to their defaults if the bar ever doesn't show up.

What changes Windows settings

Some Control Center tiles and menu items change real Windows settings, the same ones Windows' own quick settings change. They stay changed after the mod is turned off, as they would if you used Windows' quick settings:

  • Dark mode: the app and system light/dark theme (sets both to the same value)
  • Night light: on or off
  • Power mode and power plan: picking a power mode also switches the plan to Balanced, as Windows requires
  • Energy saver and Do Not Disturb
  • Brightness, default audio device, volume and mute, microphone mute, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios, Wi-Fi network and display mode (projection)

Nothing is changed unless you click the matching tile or item.

Network use

The mod only goes online for features you set up yourself (the calendar reads local .ics files only, never the network):

  • Weather, once you pick a place: the place search uses OpenStreetMap Nominatim or Open-Meteo, and the forecast comes from the service you choose (Open-Meteo, MET Norway or wttr.in) with the place's coordinates rounded to about 1 km. Turning the weather icon off stops all requests.
  • App update count (off by default, in Windhawk's settings): runs winget upgrade, which checks winget's sources online. The mod doesn't accept winget's source agreements for you. The Windows Update count is offline.

Privacy

The copy pill only says "Copied" or "Cut": it never shows what was copied, and it skips anything an app marks as private (password managers do), the same way Windows' clipboard history does.

How it runs

The bar runs in its own Windhawk process (shown as Windhawk in Task Manager), so if it ever fails, the taskbar and desktop keep working. Explorer keeps only a small hook that copies the tray icons' registrations to the bar. If that process is ended by hand, turn the mod off and on again in Windhawk to bring the bar back.

Known limitations

  • Apps without a classic menu bar use ready-made menus based on keyboard shortcuts.
  • Bluetooth lists classic (non-BLE) devices and opens Settings to connect and disconnect.
  • Power mode and energy saver use undocumented Windows functions; if Windows refuses, the tile opens the matching Settings page.
  • Screen recording uses Win+Shift+R and needs an up-to-date Snipping Tool.
  • Replying from the pill works with apps that register a notification activator with Windows; otherwise the pill opens the app and copies your text.
  • With live glass (and the bar's liquid background), the bar and panels don't show up in screenshots.
  • If Windhawk itself runs as administrator (portable mode started elevated), the bar doesn't show the tray icons: letting the shell's tray data reach an elevated bar would also let any app send it fake icons.

entry.title: Adobe Dark Menus 1.0.0
entry.content:
Adobe Dark Menus

This Windhawk mod gives Adobe apps on Windows dark menus: real menu bars, top-bar dropdowns, context menus and dropdown lists. It also colors their standard title bars to match.

Everything happens inside each app's own process. No system colors are changed and no other application is affected.

Supported apps

Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign, Dreamweaver, After Effects, Premiere Pro, Audition, Media Encoder, Bridge and Acrobat.

Screenshots

Photoshop: a dropdown list in the options bar

Illustrator: a context menu

InDesign: the Type menu

After Effects: the Window menu, with the menu bar and title bar

After Effects: the blend modes on a timeline layer

Premiere Pro: a context menu on a timeline clip

Premiere Pro: the Sequence menu, with the menu bar and title bar

Related mods

These overlap with this mod. Running them together in the same app has not been tested, so use one or the other for the apps above.

  • Photoshop Dark Menus covers Photoshop only. This mod does everything it did and reaches the other Adobe apps, so disable it if you use this one.
  • Dark mode context menus darkens the menus Windows draws, in every app and in fixed colors. It does not reach menus an app draws itself, which is why Photoshop stays light with it, or dropdown lists. This mod uses the same technique for the menus Windows draws, so exclude the Adobe apps from it in its Advanced tab.
  • After Effects Theme and Premiere Pro Theme recolor the whole interface of those two apps in palettes of their own, title bar, menu bar and menus included. They answer the same menu bar messages as this mod, so if you use one of them, exclude that app from this mod in its Advanced tab.
  • Windows 11 Custom Title Bar Colours and Auto Custom Titlebar Colors color title bars in every app. If you prefer one of them, turn off Dark Title Bars here.

Options

  • Menu Background Color: Background color (Default: #2D2D2D).
  • Menu Text Color: Text color for active items (Default: #DCDCDC).
  • Highlight Background Color: Color when hovering over an item (Default: #505050).
  • Highlight Text Color: Text color when hovering over an item (Default: #FFFFFF).
  • Separator Line Color: Color for separator lines. Set to match the background color to hide them completely (Default: #383838).
  • Disabled Text Color: Text color for disabled menu items (Default: #808080).
  • Border Color: Color of the frame around menus an app draws itself and around dropdown lists. Leave empty to keep the system frame on those menus and to use the background color on lists (Default: #2D2D2D).
  • Theme Dropdown Lists: Darken the dropdown lists an app draws itself, using the colors above (Default: on).
  • Darken Menus Windows Draws: Use Windows' dark menu theme, and paint real menu bars dark (Default: on).
  • Dark Title Bars: Color standard title bars to match the menus (Default: on).
  • Title Bar Color: Leave empty to match Menu Background Color (Default: empty).
  • Title Bar Text Color: Leave empty to let Windows choose, which dims the text on a window that is not active (Default: empty).

Colors can be given as #RRGGBB or the short #RGB form.

The colors apply to real menu bars, to menus an app draws itself (Photoshop's) and to dropdown lists. Menus Windows draws itself keep Windows' own dark colors.

How it works

Adobe's apps do not all draw their menus the same way, and sharing a library does not settle it: Illustrator and InDesign ship the same AdobeOwl.dll as Photoshop, yet Windows draws their menus and Photoshop draws its own. So the mod decides menu by menu, by whether the items are owner-drawn (MFT_OWNERDRAW).

Menus Windows draws

This is most menus in most Adobe apps. Windows paints them through its theme engine, and uxtheme has a dark variant of that drawing which is off unless a process asks for it. The mod asks for it with SetPreferredAppMode(ForceDark) and FlushMenuThemes, and puts the process back when it is disabled. This technique comes from Dark mode context menus by MGGSK, and needs Windows 10 1903 or later.

Real menu bars

Some apps, After Effects for one, have a real Win32 menu bar. The dark theme does not reach it, but Windows offers it to the window first through the undocumented WM_UAHDRAWMENU and WM_UAHDRAWMENUITEM messages, so the mod paints it from a DefWindowProc hook, in the colors above. Those messages were worked out in win32-custom-menubar-aero-theme.

Menus an app draws itself

Photoshop owner-draws its menu items with plain GDI, so the theme has nothing to attach to. Measured in Photoshop, the popups go up via TrackPopupMenuEx and each item is painted with:

  • FillRect(hdc, &rc, (HBRUSH)(COLOR_MENU + 1)) for the item background, and (HBRUSH)(COLOR_HIGHLIGHT + 1) for the hovered item. These system color pseudo-handles are resolved inside user32 from shared memory, so they bypass GetSysColor and GetSysColorBrush hooks entirely.
  • GetSysColor(COLOR_MENUTEXT / COLOR_GRAYTEXT / COLOR_HIGHLIGHTTEXT) for text.
  • Its own 1px FillRect for separator lines.

So every pixel of a menu item is reachable from inside the process:

  • FillRect / PatBlt are hooked and, while a menu item is being painted, sys-color pseudo-handles are re-resolved through this mod's own color table, and 1px fills inside a menu DC are recolored to the separator color.
  • GetSysColor / GetSysColorBrush are hooked for the menu color indices, but only while a menu item is actually being painted, that is, inside a WM_DRAWITEM of type ODT_MENU, so the app's dialogs and panels keep the system colors. "While a menu is open" would be far too broad: a menu runs a modal message loop that keeps dispatching to every other window on the thread, and an unrelated repaint would pick the menu colors up.
  • MENUINFO::hbrBack is stamped on each owner-drawn popup at WM_INITMENUPOPUP, covering the popup background that the system paints around the items. It is never stamped on a menu Windows draws, where it would put a custom background behind a theme's gutter, separators and text.
  • The popup's non-client frame is drawn kernel-side, where no user-mode hook can reach it. So the popup is subclassed at creation and the frame is repainted with the border color after it.

Dropdown lists

The dropdown lists are stock Win32 combo boxes whose list is the system's own ComboLBox window. Photoshop owner-draws the rows but takes their colors from the system, and not consistently: one list reads COLOR_WINDOWTEXT for its row text where another reads COLOR_MENUTEXT, and one fills its rows from a color it asks for where another fills them with a (HBRUSH)(COLOR_X + 1) pseudo-handle. Both routes are therefore covered, over a table that maps every background index to the background color and every text index to the text color. The list window is subclassed so that all of it applies only while that list or one of its rows is painting, which leaves every other control reading those same colors alone, including anything the app repaints in response to a selection.

A list whose rows Windows draws is left alone, the same rule as for menus. Windows fills it from a brush no hook can reach, so recoloring the text alone would leave light text on white. So is a list that stays open inside a dialog, such as the ones in the font picker, since it is part of the dialog rather than a dropdown.

Scroll arrows

A menu too tall for the screen gets scroll arrows, which the Windows kernel draws directly in light colors, below anything the dark theme or a hook can reach. So the mod paints over them straight afterward, turning the light square dark and the dark triangle light. A disabled arrow stays dimmer, since this inverts what is there rather than drawing a new one. On a menu an app draws itself, Windows draws a bare triangle instead of the square, and the mod recolors it to Menu Text Color or Disabled Text Color.

Title bars

Windows 11 lets a process color a standard title bar through DwmSetWindowAttribute, so nothing is drawn here: the mod sets DWMWA_USE_IMMERSIVE_DARK_MODE and DWMWA_CAPTION_COLOR on each top-level window with a caption, and puts them back when it is disabled. On Windows 10 2004 or later the dark flag still gives a dark title bar, without the custom color.

A window that draws its own title bar, such as the main window of Photoshop, Illustrator or InDesign, is left alone. This is checked per window, so the dialogs in those apps are still colored. The dialog's contents stay whatever color the app or Windows paints them.

Scope

Anything an app paints from its own palette rather than from a system color or the theme is out of reach, such as Photoshop's font browser and the Glyphs panel's character cells. Recoloring those would mean matching color values rather than intercepting a system one, in windows where a light fill can be the content.

A dropdown list Windows draws itself keeps its normal colors, as described above.

Long menus scroll rather than splitting into columns, because Windows turns its theme off for any menu that has columns, which leaves them light.

Source and bug reports

The mod is developed at github.com/sabergraphics/adobe-dark-menus.

Report a problem in Issues. Menu drawing depends on the environment more than most things do, so please say which Adobe app and version and which Windows version you are on, what your display scaling is, and which menu or dropdown list is wrong. A screenshot usually says more than a description does.

entry.title: Unlock "Folder In Use" 1.0.0
entry.content:
Unlock "Folder In Use"

When Explorer refuses to delete, move or rename something because it is in use ("Folder In Use" / "File In Use"), this mod finds out which processes are blocking it and lets you decide what to do.

When the warning appears, a small dialog lists the blocking processes and offers:

  • End processes and continue - terminates the processes and presses Try Again for you, so Explorer completes the original operation.
  • Only end processes - terminates the processes and leaves Explorer's warning open so you can retry yourself.
  • Cancel - does nothing.

If Explorer windows are open inside the item being processed, they are moved up one level.

How it works

  • The mod runs as a tool in its own dedicated process, not inside Explorer, so a problem in it can't affect the taskbar or the desktop.
  • The warning is detected through its internal UI Automation identifiers instead of its text, so it works with any display language.
  • The blocked item is identified from the name shown in the warning. Only the text elements of the interrupt panel itself are read (starting from the Try Again button), never the rest of the progress window, and names are compared in full. Only the selected items (or entries inside selected folders) whose name matches exactly are scanned.
  • The matched paths are listed in the details of the prompt, so you can see what was scanned before ending anything.
  • Blockers are found with the Restart Manager, the current directory of each process, and the system handle table. Every Explorer process is excluded.
  • Processes are opened while scanning and terminated through those same handles, so a process that exits and whose PID is reused is never terminated by mistake.

Notes

  • Ending a process terminates it immediately. Unsaved work in that process is lost.
  • Elevated or protected processes can't be ended from this mod.
  • If the item named in the warning can't be matched with the selection, the mod says so and does nothing.
  • The mod relies on internal details of Explorer's operation dialog, which may change in future Windows versions.

Settings

  • Modern dialogs - use task-dialog style windows instead of classic message boxes.
  • Show message when nothing is found - show a dialog when the blocked item or its blocking process could not be identified (enabled by default).

entry.title: WinTips OSD 1.5.1
entry.content:
• Ctrl+Insert, Shift+Insert and Shift+Delete now raise the copy, paste and cut tips, not just Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V / Ctrl+X, since terminal windows still lean on the legacy set. Ctrl+Shift+Delete stays silent because browsers and editors use it for something else.
  • Fixed a card-shaped ghost of the previous tip bleeding into the new card's blurred backdrop when two tips appear in quick succession; the old card is now flushed out of the composed frame before the screen is captured.
  • Readme and settings text reworked, including a note that the card also works on Windows 10 and both shortcut sets in the copy / paste / cut descriptions.

entry.title: Smooth Scroll for Win32 1.0.4
entry.content:
• Scroll File Explorer's folder view by pixels through Explorer's own pan path instead of UI Automation, with the native distance per notch (at most a third of the view). It works in grouped views and no longer brings background windows to the front.
  • Scroll Task Manager and Control Panel DirectUI pages smoothly by pixels; Control Panel pages no longer ignore the wheel from time to time.
  • Draw tree views, list boxes, multi-line text boxes and Details-view lists at pixel offsets, so they glide instead of jumping a line at a time. RichEdit boxes and icon views scroll by pixels directly.
  • Stop the legacy list box animation from playing underneath the mod's.
  • Pace frames with the compositor clock at the monitor's full refresh rate.
  • Ease Smooth Only mode like WinUI and finish every scroll at an even pace.
  • Remove the Scroll Multiplier and Smooth Speed settings; the distance follows the Windows "lines per notch" setting, which halves it for anyone who used the previous default multiplier (2x).

entry.title: Mac Island & Dock 3.1.0
entry.content:
Arranging the pill

  • "Change the order with Ctrl + drag on the island" (Style tab, on by default): hold Ctrl and drag an item on the island (Island, Fixed or Bar) to another place, or into another notch (the notches start again when the bell's notch changes, as from the settings); with the app in front having its own order, that one changes. While Ctrl is held with the mouse on the pill, its items jiggle; the item held is dimmed, its icon follows the mouse and a line shows where it goes. An idea of Thiago Silva's.
  • The settings' preview shows that its icons are dragged: for 10 seconds when the settings open, and when the mouse comes onto it, the icons jiggle, a hand carries one past the next one and back, and the line under it says so (Ctrl + drag on the island too). Pressing an icon stops it; with animations off, only the line.

Panels and your commands

  • "Open panels with the mouse" (Look tab, off by default, #6654): a panel opens when the mouse rests on its item for a moment, without taking the focus from the app in front, and closes a moment after the mouse leaves the pill and the panel. Only items whose click just opens a panel do it; the media buttons, a timer's start, a pinned command, the microphone, the quick actions and a power button that runs its only action still need a click. A click on the item, or inside the panel, keeps it open like a clicked one; moving to another such item switches to its panel.
  • Files, folders, shortcuts or a web link (http or https) dropped on the commands' icon or a command's button become your commands, each a button on the pill, named after what it opens (anywhere on the pill when the shelf is off or doesn't take them; only with the commands on the pill). Only the path or link is kept; one already there is just put on the pill (#6654).

Look

  • "Island font" and "Clock font" (Look tab): a font from your PC for the pill's and the panels' texts, and one of its own for the clock on the pill and in the calendar; Windows' font dialog, per profile (#6648, #6609).
  • "Items in the bar" (Look tab): Automatic (as before), at its left end, in the middle or at its right end (#6922).
  • "Bar: items keep their side of the clock" (Look tab): with the clock in the middle, the items keep their side of the clock, at the screen's corners, as items come and go (#6639).
  • The calendar's clock and date are centered, and "Events in the calendar" (on by default) can leave only the clock and the month (#6609).
  • The visualizer can come only for the apps you choose ("Apps that bring the visualizer", from what played and what was heard), also players without Windows' media controls, its bars following that app's sound; sliders "Bars' height", "Bars' width" and "Room between the bars" (#6204, #6924). The bars are now seven, the middle one the tallest: the sound reaches it first and goes out to the ones at its sides a moment later, like a wave, with the beat (a beat kicks the middle up) or smooth.
  • The panels' scroll bars (the apps launcher, notes, tasks, notifications and the other long lists) can be dragged by their thumb, and a click above or below it moves a page; they get wider under the mouse, like Windows 11's.
  • With "Light and shadow like macOS 27": the control center's sliders are thin lines with icons that grow with the level (the sun turns) and bounce as it changes, the mouse following the same line; buttons and tiles that are on show a white circle with the icon in the accent color. Over the Liquid Glass, a long pill's ends fade into the glass's tint, inside its round shape, instead of a dark block. By Thiago Silva.
  • "Hide a notch with nothing in it" (Style tab, #6651): a notch with no items disappears, the one with the bell too; it comes back when an item or a notification comes to it, and while items are dragged between the notches in the settings. The strip kept on the screen stays the same.
  • "Ring with the battery's charge" (Animations tab, #6071): a ring along the edge shows the charge, on the battery's notch or the pill, or on every notch; green above 40%, yellow down to 20%, red below; not as the line, nor on the Bar style.

On the pill

  • "Lyrics as an icon" (What's playing tab, #6684): a single icon while the song has lyrics; a click opens them.
  • "Always on the pill, even with nothing playing" (#6905): the note stays on the pill with nothing playing.
  • "Only play and pause" for the pill's media buttons (#6907).
  • Touch keyboard (#6160), Windows Settings and Win+X (#6922) buttons, in the control center and on the pill, off until you choose them.
  • A click on the network's speed opens a Network tab in the usage panel: the last minute's download and upload graphs, their peaks and a Task Manager button (#6932).
  • "See-through only on the desktop" (Look tab, #7005): the see-through bar goes back to its usual look while a window is maximized on its monitor.
  • "Clock against the screen's edge" (Hiding tab, #6997): the small pill with the time touches the edge, straight on that side and as thin as its text.
  • "Long notification texts scroll under the mouse" (Banners tab, #6200): a notification's text stays on one line and scrolls to its end and back, instead of opening on up to three lines.
  • Hibernate in the power button's menu, only when Windows allows hibernation (#6886); each power action can be turned off, with only one on the button runs it, and asking before restarting, shutting down or signing out is an option (System tab, #6609).

Hiding

  • "The minimize arrow keeps the island open" (Hiding tab, #6725): with the line on, the minimize arrow can keep that monitor's island open until it's clicked again; Win+J still minimizes it.
  • "The edge zone as wide as the pill" (Hiding tab, #6525): the edge zone that brings the pill back follows the pill's width, also with the line invisible.
  • "Shortcut: let clicks through the pill" (Hiding tab, #6718): a recorded shortcut lets clicks pass through the pill to what's under it while it stays shown; a bubble says when it's on.
  • "Stay over borderless full-screen apps" (Hiding tab, #6740, off by default): the island stays over borderless full-screen apps; games in exclusive full screen still draw over it (README note on performance and anti-cheat).

Launcher, media and more

  • "Apps (launcher)" (Apps and tools tab, off by default, #7058): a pill item whose panel lists the shell's Apps folder (what Start lists: shortcuts and the Store's apps, each once), read on a thread when it opens (again after a minute), with a search box (case and accents ignored; Enter opens the first one, Esc clears), the favorites first (a star on each row, kept per account) and all apps in Start's order; icons load for the rows in view only; a shortcut's row has a button that shows its program in Explorer; apps start as the user and unelevated when Windhawk runs as administrator.
  • "Media panel style" (What's playing tab, #7042): the usual look (default), Pixel (as Android 13-15 draws it: the cover filling the card under its shade, a smooth wavy progress line moving while playing and flat when paused, the play button turning from a circle into a rounded square), One UI (a card in the cover's color, plain buttons), Windows 11 (the Quick Settings card, the cover on the right), or only the cover with the buttons over it; long titles and artists scroll in the panel in every look; "Only the cover on the pill" (#7038); "Media buttons size" for the pill's previous / play / next and "Media panel size" up to 200% (#7041), kept within the pill's height and the screen.
  • "What's playing on the minimized line" (Hiding tab, off by default, #7045): while something plays, the minimized line becomes a thin pill with the song's cover and the visualizer's bars (the bars run only while it shows); the mouse on it opens the island.
  • One switch for each status notice: the charger, the low battery, Bluetooth audio, "Do not disturb" (on by default, as before) and the desktop switched to, with its number and name (off by default, #7091, #7014).
  • "The bell opens Windows' notification center" and "World clocks inside the clock" (a list under the mouse on the clock), both off by default (#7089).
  • Virtual desktops renamed with a pencil in their list (Windows 11 24H2 and later, through the shell's own desktop service, on a thread; the pencil stays away where the service isn't there).
  • Separator lines on the pill: a "+ Line" chip in the settings' preview strip (with a hint, a glow when a What's new link or the settings search for "separator"/"line" leads to it) adds one, glowing on the pill for a moment, dragged between two groups (Island, Fixed and Bar, upright too), a click takes it away; "dock.separator" (off by default): a thin line in the dock between the pinned apps and the others, drawn only, the taskbar's buttons untouched.
  • A hex box (#RRGGBB) under the buttons of the color dialog every color of the island's settings opens.
  • "Weather icons" (Tools tab): emoji (default, as before), the chosen icon pack's pictures, Meteocons (MIT, in color) or Weather Icons (SIL OFL 1.1), downloaded once when chosen like the icon packs; emoji for a sky a set has no picture for.
  • A keyboard shortcut for each of your commands (recorded in the command's editor, up to 16, clashes with the island's shortcuts and other commands refused; the keyboard hook stays off with none) (#6165).
  • "Show VLC 3 from its window's title" (What's playing tab, off by default, #6164): VLC 3 publishes nothing to Windows' media controls, so while it makes sound its window's title shows as what's playing, with play/pause, previous and next pressed as the buttons of its taskbar thumbnail (a posted WM_APPCOMMAND crashes VLC 3.0's Qt filter); VLC has its own chip among the media apps (chosen, it shows with another app playing; another app chosen keeps its place), its program icon stands in for the cover on the pill and in the panel, and with another player paused too the one that played last shows; no cover or time (VLC 3 tells neither).
  • The Fixed style and the Bar have their own list of icons per app (items, clock and order while that app is in front; the place and size stay the Island style's only) (#6162).

Fixes

  • The Bar no longer flickers at the screen's corners with apps that round them (Roundly, Monitor Rounded Edges): windows that let clicks through no longer count as covering the island (#6954).
  • Song lyrics: a song not found by its exact title and artist is looked for again with the bare title and the first artist; "Artist - Topic" and "Artist • Album" are read as the artist (SimpMusic and YouTube Music, #6612).
  • Brightness of external monitors (DDC/CI): the calls go one at a time, and if Windows stops in the middle of one (a blue screen some monitors, docks or hubs cause), the island turns this brightness off at the next start and says so in a notice; it stays off, whatever a profile or a backup put back holds, until it's turned on again in the settings (#6966).
  • On Insider builds with Windows' newer taskbar, which has none of the parts the dock styles, the taskbar is left as Windows draws it instead of cut at the bottom and restyled over and over (#6888).
  • Calendars from .ics files: an event in a time zone of its own (TZID) shows at your local time, whichever way the file names the zone: Windows' name (Outlook), an IANA one (Apple and most others) or a zone the file itself describes. A zone nothing knows is read as local, with a line in the log (#7020).
  • Apple Music shows once in the mixer and its slider changes what you hear: the programs of one Store app (Apple Music plays through a helper, AMPLibraryAgent.exe) are one entry, with the app's name and icon. The same in the control panel's mixer (#7043).
  • Panels too tall for a short screen or a large scale now stop at the screen's edge and scroll, instead of being cut. The calendar keeps its month whole, its rows shorter and its big clock gone if needed, and scrolls its events; the lyrics and the shelf shorten their own lists (#7046).
  • Recycle Bin: when Windows isn't ready to count or watch it (right after the PC starts, for example), the island tries again ten seconds later instead of keeping an old count, and it counts the bin again each time its panel opens; "Empty the bin" also works while the count is unknown (#7048).
  • Battery charging between 85% and 94%: the charging battery shows, instead of the font's energy saver battery, the glyph right after the charging ones (#6922).
  • Wi-Fi: the network's name and signal are read when it connects (and every five minutes), the signal's changes coming from Windows' own notices, instead of reading the network on each change: on newer Windows 11 builds each read counts as using the location, which kept Windows' location icon on.
  • Dock with the "Disable grouping on the taskbar" mod: the app ID's suffix that mod adds for each extra window is left out, so those windows get the app's sharp, large icons (#7029).
  • Dock: a taskbar button reused for an app opened right after another one closed kept the closed app's sharp icon when none was found for the new one (the Riot Client showed FileZilla's, reported on Discord). That picture is no longer left on it (also when the taskbar changes the button's picture a moment before its app ID), and an app the shell has no icon for gets its program's or its window's icon, its window found also when the app sets its ID on its process (like TeamViewer).
  • The "Taskbar" setting says the dock is for Windows 11 only: on Windows 10 the taskbar stays as it is and only the island works (#7059).
  • Media panel: two sources of the same app (two Chrome tabs, for example) show each one's title on its chip instead of the app's name twice.
  • Drawing: a frame lost because the graphics driver couldn't make pictures smaller the smooth way is drawn again at once the plain way, the panels in their own window too.
  • Weather: when the weather service doesn't answer, the log says why (WinHTTP's error), for blocked connections.
  • "Do not disturb" notice: it comes when you turn it on or off, not each time Windows turns it on by itself for an app in full screen or a game (its automatic rules); the notice follows the profile you chose, Windows' state only when that can't be read (#7091).
  • Tray icons answer clicks again with UAC off or on the Administrator account: 3.0 refused clicks from an elevated island to elevated apps, and with UAC off every process is elevated, explorer too; the refusal now applies only when explorer isn't elevated (a real UAC line), and the log says when it refuses (#7092).
  • Calendar reminders: one that came due with the notifications list open, a notification arriving or a panel opening over it waits and shows; one the PC slept through shows once as missed (up to 12 hours, an all-day event's until its day ends); the reminder's sound follows the island's "Do not disturb" that silences reminders (#6156).
  • Taskbar progress filling the pill: the log names the programs it comes from as a fill starts.
  • Dock: the bubble drawn for an app's count (sharp when magnified) takes the color of the app's own badge, the average of its solid pixels without the number's white (Telegram's gray for archived chats, for example), instead of always red (#7095).
  • Tray: an app asking where its icon is right after adding it (Electron's tray.getBounds() after new Tray(), as Medal does) got 0x0 with the taskbar's tray hidden, since the island places an icon a frame later; Medal then removed the icon and quit when its window closed. When neither the island's places nor the taskbar answer, a known icon now gets the island's middle until its real place comes (#7106, from the reporter's patch).
  • Lyrics: the lyrics item steps aside when the pill's title already shows the line sung now (the swap, or a player that writes the line in its own title), compared without case or surrounding spaces (#7105).
  • Dock: the room above the icons is 12 instead of 8 at 46 px (in proportion to the icon size), so the icons sit closer to the middle with the dots' room below (#7103).
  • Switching a monitor's profile starts and stops what that island shows (net speed, weather, AI usage, updates; at start too, the watches only another monitor's profile wants); what's playing stops being watched once media, its buttons, lyrics and the visualizer are all off; a paused download no longer redraws its fill on every frame; a shutdown in the middle of a call to a monitor no longer turns external monitors' brightness (DDC/CI) off with a false crash notice at the next start; an icon folder or a notification's picture on another PC's share no longer stalls the island; clipboard text without its end is read only up to its block.

Other

  • The Vietnamese texts were reviewed to sound more natural, by caotu2k5.
  • The file's header has the GPL-3.0 notice (the mod was already under GPL-3.0), with caliberda's copyright and m417z's for the taskbar XAML part, and the README a License section.
  • The README has a "Not planned, and why" section, with how to try one of the island's yourself.

entry.title: Musician's Toolkit 1.0.0
entry.content:
Musician's Toolkit

A chord library, a tuner, a metronome, a strumming trainer, a circle of fifths, a tap tempo and a note drill, for guitar, ukulele and piano. All of it lives in one small panel that stays on top of your other windows, so you can keep it beside your DAW, tab app or video lesson.

Press Win+Y to open it and pick a tool from the menu in the top left. Ctrl+Tab cycles through them. Close it with the x, with Esc, or with the shortcut again (the shortcut itself is under Settings > Shortcut). If you would rather it close whenever you click elsewhere, turn that on under Settings > Placement.

Chords

Start typing and the chord appears as you go: the list narrows with every letter, and the one you settle on is drawn underneath.

  • Guitar and ukulele get a fretboard, with barre positions, open strings and muted strings all marked.
  • Piano lights up the keys you would hold.
  • Fingerings - the arrow keys, or the slider under the diagram, step through the other ways to play the same chord.
  • Hear it - the speaker on the card plays the chord, strummed on an acoustic guitar or played on a piano.

Tap Tempo

Tap the big circle with the mouse, a touchpad or Space, and the panel works the tempo out from the timing. The bars beneath it show how steady you are being, so you can watch yourself settle.

  • Half and Double jump to half time or double time.
  • Reset clears the taps and starts a fresh count.
  • The scroll wheel nudges the BPM a step at a time.

Metronome

Set a meter and a tempo, and you have a click that keeps time while you play.

  • Meters - the chips cover 4/4, 3/4, 2/4, 5/4, 6/8, 7/8, 9/8 and 12/8; the steppers reach the rest, such as 5/8, 11/8 or 7/16.
  • Sound - a bright click marks the downbeat, a lower one each beat and a soft tick the subdivisions, so the bar reads as a pulse.
  • Tempo - the arrows or the wheel step the BPM, or click the number (or just start typing) and enter an exact one. Enter sets it, Esc leaves it as it was.
  • Background - the metronome keeps playing after you close the panel, which is what you want mid-piece. Switch it off under Settings > Metronome.

Tuner

Play a note and the needle tells you where you are. The display names the note and the arc shows how far off it is, so you can watch it settle in.

  • Tunings - standard, drop and open guitar tunings, several basses, ukuleles, mandolins, banjos, the violin family, lap steel, dobro and bouzouki.
  • Anything else - the tuner falls back to a chromatic scale, so a restrung or homemade instrument tunes just as well.
  • Pitch - concert pitch is adjustable from 415 to 466 Hz (A4 = 440 by default) under Settings > Tuner.

Strumming Pattern

Lay out a bar of strums on a one-measure grid and hear it back in the same acoustic voice as the chord library, in time with the tempo.

  • Pattern - the list is grouped by the grid each pattern is written in, and holds the ones people actually play: downstrokes, steady eighths, D DU D DU, the folk D DU UDU, D D D U D U, the reggae skank, a muted chug, a shuffle and straight sixteenths, plus the 2+2+3 and 3+2+2 groupings that odd meters are counted in. Picking a pattern moves the grid chips to the grid it was notated in, so it arrives ready to play.
  • Grid - click a cell to cycle rest, down, up, muted down and muted up, or walk the bar with the arrow keys and type one letter: D down, U up, X muted downstroke, M muted upstroke, R rest.
  • Marks - A accents a stroke, G turns it into a ghost note and T ties it into the next cell so it rings on past the beat. C clears the bar. None of the keys need a modifier, and every one of them is hinted along the foot of the card.
  • Strings - pick guitar or ukulele, then fret a chord from the list or leave the strings open, so the pattern rings with a voicing you would really use.
  • Sound - open strums ring out, palm mute damps them into a rhythm and muted turns every stroke into a scratch. A stroke written as a mute stays a scratch whatever the sound is set to.
  • Meter - 4/4, 3/4, 2/4, 5/4, 6/8, 7/8, 9/8 or 12/8. The grid chips read against the meter's own unit, so 6/8 counts in eighths and its chips offer 1/8, 1/16, triplet and 1/32.
  • Practice - count-in, loop, and practice mode, which lifts the tempo a little at the start of every bar until you reach your target.
  • Tempo - the minus and plus buttons nudge the BPM, or click the number (or start typing) to enter one. Enter sets it, Esc cancels.

Circle of Fifths

All twelve keys around a ring, each a fifth on from the last. Click either ring to select a key and hear it, and the rest of the wheel reads back from that selection.

  • Wheel - the majors on the outer ring, their relative minors inside on the same spoke. Scroll or use the arrow keys to walk the circle, and press Up / Down (or M) to hop between the rings without leaving the fifth.
  • Chords of the key - I, IV and V carry their numeral outside, ii, iii and vi inside, so the six chords you would normally play are always in view. A minor key lights them the other way round.
  • Centre - the tonic and its seven notes. A minor key uses the natural minor, so A minor reads A B C D E F G rather than the major scale of A.
  • Theory - the key signature, the relative and parallel keys, and the mode built on each degree.
  • Instrument - pick guitar, piano or ukulele (or press Tab) to hear the scales and chords in that voice.
  • Hear it - click one of the seven diatonic chips, or press 1–7.

Note Trainer

A drill for knowing your instrument. A note name appears, the microphone listens and you play it before the clock runs out.

  • Round - Space starts and stops, and each prompt gets its own timer of 2–20 seconds per note, set under Settings > Note trainer.
  • Listening - a note counts the moment it settles in tune, and the readout under the prompt shows what the microphone hears right now.
  • Feedback - a correct note flashes green with the points it earned; a miss shows the note it was looking for before the next prompt appears.
  • Score - a quick answer is worth up to twice a slow one, and the panel keeps your streak, best streak and accuracy. R resets it.
  • Voices - Tab cycles guitar, ukulele and piano, and N (or the Naturals chip) keeps the drill to the white notes.

Keyboard Shortcuts

  • Win+Y - open or close the panel.
  • Ctrl+Tab - switch tools.
  • Tab - switch instruments.
  • Up / Down - move through search results, step the metronome, hop between the rings of the circle.
  • Left / Right - step through fingerings, halve or double a tap tempo, change the metronome's meter.
  • D U X M R, A G T, C - lay strokes in the strumming grid, add accents, ghosts and ties, clear the bar.
  • Esc - clear the search, or close the panel when the search is empty.

Settings

  • Startup - the tool and instrument the panel opens with.
  • Appearance - follow Windows or fix light or dark, pick an accent colour, set the opacity.
  • Placement - corner, monitor, fine offsets, and whether the panel closes when it loses focus.
  • Shortcut - the key and modifiers that open the panel.
  • Metronome - volume, background playback, default meter and subdivision.
  • Chords - hide the finger numbers.
  • Tap tempo - how long a pause resets the taps, and whether Space or Enter count as taps.
  • Tuner - reference pitch.
  • Strumming - default grid, count-in, loop, and the practice ramp.
  • Circle of fifths - which ring opens, and whether selecting a key plays its scale.
  • Note trainer - seconds per note, chromatic or naturals.

The chord library comes from chords-db by David Rubert (MIT). It is packed into the mod, so there is nothing to download and no internet connection needed.

entry.title: Turn Off Display Without Sleep 1.0.0
entry.content:
Turn Off Display Without Sleep

On Modern Standby (S0ix) laptops, user-initiated actions—such as clicking "Sleep" in the Start menu, pressing a power button configured for sleep, or invoking display-off shortcuts—instruct the Windows Power Dependency Coordinator (PDC) to transition to sleep. This suspends desktop apps (DAM) and disconnects mobile hotspots.

However, when Windows turns the display off through a natural idle timeout, Modern Standby keeps audio streams, downloads, and mobile hotspots running indefinitely.

Turn Off Display Without Sleep triggers this natural idle path on demand:

  1. Instant Pitch-Black Screen: Creates an instant fullscreen topmost blackout overlay across all monitors so the screen appears turned off immediately.
  2. Dynamic 1-Second Timeout: Saves your current timeouts and temporarily injects a 1-second display idle timeout (VIDEOIDLE) into the active power scheme. Windows naturally powers down the monitors via the idle path within ~1–2 seconds without suspending background tasks.
  3. Automatic Restoration: When hardware display-off (GUID_CONSOLE_DISPLAY_STATE == 0) is detected, the original display timeout is immediately restored, and the overlay is dismissed.
  4. Direct-to-Desktop Wake or Optional Lock:
    • By default, your workstation stays unlocked so you return directly to your active desktop upon waking the screen—no PIN or Windows Hello delay.
    • If desired, enable Lock workstation after display turns off to silently lock the session in the dark once the screen is powered down.
  5. Failsafe Watchdog: If the display does not power down within 3 seconds (e.g. due to mouse movement or an application holding ES_DISPLAY_REQUIRED / active video playback), the overlay is removed and timeouts are restored automatically.

What happens on an unclean exit?

The 1-second timeout only exists in the power plan for the 1–3 seconds between trigger and display power-down. If the tool process is forcefully terminated during those few seconds (system crash, power loss, or process kill), the 1-second timeout remains in the active power plan until the mod runs again and automatically restores it from storage. If the screen turns off after one second of idle while the mod is disabled or uninstalled, simply re-adjust "Turn off my screen after" in Windows Settings.

Prerequisites

To allow this mod to take control of lid-close or power button events, Windows native actions must be set to "Do nothing" (0) so Windows does not trigger its built-in sleep transition.

Run this in an elevated Command Prompt:

powercfg /setacvalueindex SCHEME_CURRENT SUB_BUTTONS PBUTTONACTION 0
powercfg /setdcvalueindex SCHEME_CURRENT SUB_BUTTONS PBUTTONACTION 0
powercfg /setacvalueindex SCHEME_CURRENT SUB_BUTTONS LIDACTION 0
powercfg /setdcvalueindex SCHEME_CURRENT SUB_BUTTONS LIDACTION 0
powercfg /setactive SCHEME_CURRENT

Warning: With the lid action set to "Do nothing", closing the lid and putting the laptop into a backpack or bag will keep the system running (until the regular system sleep timeout). Make sure to explicitly sleep or shut down your laptop before bagging it.

Reverting prerequisites

If you disable or uninstall this mod and want to restore the native sleep behavior:

powercfg /setacvalueindex SCHEME_CURRENT SUB_BUTTONS PBUTTONACTION 1
powercfg /setdcvalueindex SCHEME_CURRENT SUB_BUTTONS PBUTTONACTION 1
powercfg /setacvalueindex SCHEME_CURRENT SUB_BUTTONS LIDACTION 1
powercfg /setdcvalueindex SCHEME_CURRENT SUB_BUTTONS LIDACTION 1
powercfg /setactive SCHEME_CURRENT

Triggers

  • Keyboard Shortcut: Default is Win+Alt+L. Customizable in settings.
  • Lid Close: Triggered automatically when closing the laptop lid. Requires native lid close action set to "Do nothing".
  • Power Button: Supported on devices where the power button is exposed via HID System Control (Usage Page 0x01, Usages 0x80/0x81/0x82 or 0x0D, such as Microsoft Surface Pro). Requires native power button action set to "Do nothing". Not detectable on laptops with ACPI-only power buttons, use Trigger hotkey or Lid close instead.
  • External Window Message: Broadcast WindhawkScreenOffNoSleep_Trigger from external scripts or taskbar shortcuts.

Settings

  • Lock workstation after display turns off: Silently lock in the dark after screen is off.
  • Trigger hotkey: Global hotkey to turn off display (default Win+Alt+L).
  • Turn off display on lid close: Trigger when laptop lid closes.
  • Turn off display on power button (HID devices): Capture HID power button events.

entry.title: Siri Plus Launchpad 1.1.0
entry.content:
New

  • Search everything (Original Siri): typing in "Search" lists apps, actions, folders and files together in one list, like Spotlight. "Show all" opens the category with what you typed. Can be turned off.
  • Windows Settings in the search: about 60 Settings pages (Display, Startup apps, Personalization, Windows Update, Wi-Fi...) are found by name or by what you would type to look for them, and open with Enter. They follow the Actions tab being on.
  • Right-click a file or folder found by the search: "Open file location" shows it in File Explorer.
  • Calculator: type a calculation (2+2, 15% * 80, (3+4)^2) and its result shows first; Enter copies it. Start with = or calc to always calculate (=5-3). Can be turned off.
  • New settings window in the style of macOS System Settings: it grows out of the bar, its content comes in step by step, and it switches off in place like an old TV (CRT) when closed. A search field sits on top of the sections.
  • Settings reorganized into 12 sections (General, Appearance, Custom theme, Search, Siri bar, Results size, Window and Fullscreen, Animations, Keyboard shortcuts, Apps and icons, Performance, Backup and defaults), with group titles and a short description for every setting.
  • Settings that have no effect with your current choices are dimmed in gray, say why, and turn blue again when they can be used; whole sections (such as Custom theme) dim the same way.
  • Glass style: Translucent glass (flat glass with a soft live blur, light on the PC) or Liquid glass (the background bends at the edges, Floating and Original Siri modes); the description follows the choice.
  • Performance: Light mode works with any theme (no liquid glass, no live blur, no blur behind menus, no shadows, at most 60 fps, calmer animations), a frame rate limit, and an experimental option to draw with the processor instead of the graphics card.
  • Clear glass theme: the selection in menus can be Glass, Colored (like macOS) or Frosted color, with a color of your choice.
  • Floating power button: left or right of the bar.
  • Create desktop shortcut in an app's right-click menu (also for several selected apps).
  • Floating mode: the category icon in the bar turns into a back arrow, as in Original Siri.
  • The "..." button turns into a soft gear under the mouse.
  • Blinking text cursor in the bar and in the settings search.
  • Simplified Chinese (follows Windows, or pick it in Language).

Changed

  • A single "Change icon..." option: it opens your icon folder (asked for the first time). The single-file picker was removed.
  • New defaults: Siri bar height 96 px; floating power button off. Users who changed these keep their values.
  • Settings that only apply to some modes say so in their description, in Windhawk's settings too.

Fixed

  • Clear areas of the glass let the mouse through, which made the settings button and the result rows slow to respond or skip; they now answer right away.
  • Folder, file and color pickers are no longer covered by the launcher or its glass.
  • Backspace with an empty search no longer switches to Applications.
  • Faster drawing: shadows, gradients, settings reads and the blur behind menus are cached, and the settings rows are only rebuilt when they change.

entry.title: Logitech Battery Tray 0.1.2
entry.content:
Logitech Battery Tray

Battery indicators for supported Logitech devices, with automatic discovery, charging status and optional percentage labels.

Screenshots

Horizontal taskbar with a battery tooltip:

Vertical taskbar with stacked device indicators:

Compatibility and scope

Windows 10/11: standard notification icons provide the compatibility backend. On supported Windows 11 x64/ARM64 taskbars, Auto uses native XAML battery buttons on the primary taskbar. Unrecognized taskbar layouts use notification icons instead of an overlay. 32-bit Windows uses notification icons only. Native icons show the percentage and a tooltip; charging is green. Windows controls their placement and overflow visibility. XAML placement, button styling and click-to-open settings do not apply to notification icons.

Select Native notification icons to test or force the compatibility backend. Successful compilation is not a claim of runtime testing on every Windows build.

Unlike BT Battery Monitor (generic Bluetooth battery reporting), this mod reads Logitech G HUB and Logitech HID++ battery data, including supported USB receivers. It runs in Explorer because its optional XAML backend modifies Explorer's own taskbar visual tree. No pairing, firmware or device configuration is changed.

Battery sources

The XAML backend uses built-in Segoe Fluent Icons and standard Windows buttons and tooltips. Its battery glyph changes with the reported charge level, with an optional smaller icon indicating the device type.

G HUB must be running to use its data; direct HID++ reading works independently. The G HUB client connects only to 127.0.0.1:9010. It requests /devices/list and /battery/<deviceId>/state, subscribes to /battery/state/changed, and uses a persistent query connection with a 30-second fallback poll by default. Failed connections retry with exponential backoff, up to 60 seconds. Events update readings independently of fallback polling. Updates cannot arrive earlier than G HUB reports them.

The HID++ provider reads compatible Logitech devices through Unifying, Bolt, LIGHTSPEED, USB and accessible Bluetooth HID++ interfaces. It supports battery features 0x1004, 0x1000, 0x1001, 0x1F20 and legacy HID++ 1.0 registers. Voltage-based and coarse readings are marked with an approximation sign. G HUB readings take priority when available. Models using other protocols may not report a battery level; support for every Logitech model is not guaranteed.

Discovery and language

All detected, supported battery devices are shown by default. No model-specific rules are shipped. Optional visibility rules match a device name or model; empty rules are ignored, * and ? are supported, and the last match wins. The user-facing tooltip contains no internal IDs or provider diagnostics. Tooltip translations follow the preferred Windows UI languages, with English as fallback. Reload the mod after changing Windows display languages. The mod description and settings default to English, with Russian localization for Windhawk's Russian interface. Tooltips follow Windows UI languages independently.

When G HUB stops, HID++ provides readings for compatible devices. Fully disconnected devices are hidden; confirmed charging remains visible even when the device is inactive. Repeated explicit HID++ offline reports and failed G HUB queries use a five-second grace. Missing HID++ replies are treated as an unknown connection state, retaining the last reading for up to thirty seconds of failed communication. A hidden HID++ device needs two valid readings at least one second apart before reappearing, with no intervening failed reading. These windows absorb temporary failures, not indefinitely cache charging state. Provider requests run outside the taskbar UI thread. Reconnection is automatic. Windows HID arrival/removal and receiver notifications trigger rediscovery; three-minute scanning also handles devices that do not send connection events. An already-open device that missed its initial probe is retried separately, with increasing delays up to 60 seconds, without rescanning every HID interface. Event-capable HID++ features use the configured fallback interval. ADC (0x1F20) and legacy register devices use a two-second poll because they may lack events. Presence confirmation temporarily uses a short interval to avoid delayed recovery. The XAML UI updates on data, size and theme changes, without a periodic repaint. In Auto mode, a transient XAML failure must last 30 seconds before notification icons appear; missing taskbar symbols select the compatibility backend immediately. While the native fallback is active, unsuccessful XAML attachment attempts back off up to 60 seconds. Layout, DPI and theme changes trigger an immediate retry. On supported left/right taskbars, indicators are stacked vertically and the percentage is placed below the icons. Button width follows the taskbar width; the configured button width applies to horizontal taskbars only.

Credits and limitations

Disable direct HID++ reading before updating device firmware. Persistent HID handles are read-only; write access is opened only for each battery/probe request. This reduces sharing conflicts, but cannot guarantee compatibility with tools that require exclusive access. Firmware updates with this mod have not been tested.

The G HUB interface is unofficial and may change with G HUB updates. XAML root access is adapted from Taskbar Folder Menus by sb4ssman: https://github.com/ramensoftware/windhawk-mods/blob/main/mods/taskbar-folder-menus.wh.cpp G HUB protocol: https://github.com/someweirdhuman/LogiBAT G HUB events: https://github.com/bmrussell/LGBattery Icons: https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/apps/design/iconography/segoe-fluent-icons-font HID++: https://github.com/Logitech/cpg-docs/tree/master/hidpp20 Battery features: https://github.com/pwr-Solaar/Solaar

entry.title: Classic Explorerframe for 24H2 and later 1.0
entry.content:
Restores classic Explorerframe.dll on Windows 11 24H2 and later. This allows to restore the toolbars in the folder windows, including the menubar, the Classic Explorer toolbar from OpenShell package, Quero toolbar and the toolbars provided by the mod Flexible Explorer Toolbars Deluxe, such as the Search bar.

Note that to enable the menubar you need to install in addition the mod ExplorerFrame and menubar fixes fork.

This mod downloads the classic Explorerframe.dll from the Microsoft's symbols server and stores it into the mod's storage. You need a working internet access at the first mod's activation.

Restart Explorer after enabling or disabling the mod. At the first activation the file is downloaded in the background, so wait a few seconds before restarting, otherwise the mod takes effect only at the following Explorer start.

Mods that hook ExplorerFrame.dll and happen to load before this mod might have no effect, because folder windows don't use the copy they hooked.

entry.title: Desktop Snowfall 1.0
entry.content:
Desktop Snowfall

Snow falls over your desktop. Flakes land on the top edge of your windows and on the taskbar and slowly build up snow drifts of different heights.

  • The snow follows the window. Toss a window up and the snow flies up in loose clumps and lands back with a little bounce. Pull it down or shrink it from the top and the snow hangs in the air for a moment before it falls back onto the window.
  • Make a window narrower and the snow on the cut-off part falls down.
  • Optionally, the snow slides off windows moved sideways: it stays where it is, and the part the window slides out from under falls down.
  • Sweep the snow off with the mouse cursor - it falls down to the windows below or to the taskbar.
  • The wind blows powder off the drifts, and now and then a lump slides off a window corner.
  • Works with the default taskbar, an auto-hidden taskbar (the snow rides along when it slides in and out) and custom taskbar styles (for example, floating "dock" themes of the Windows 11 Taskbar Styler mod): the snow lies on the visible taskbar parts.

The snow is drawn on the GPU on a transparent, click-through overlay, so it never gets in the way of mouse input. The overlay is hidden automatically while a fullscreen app (a game or a video) is in the foreground. The mod runs in its own process, separately from Explorer.

The overlay is redrawn every frame, so the snow keeps the GPU a little busy even when nothing else on the screen changes. On a laptop running on battery, a lower frame rate limit (for example, 30) saves power.
